items.question: Trace the rise of Harshavardhana and assess his achievement in unifying northern India. Why did his expansion fail in the south?
items.modelAnswer:
**Harshavardhana (r. c. 606–647 CE)** of the **Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty** rose from the small kingdom of **Thanesar** to become the last great sovereign of northern India.

**Rise:** Born in **590 CE at Thanesar**, Harsha ascended the throne at **sixteen (c. 606 CE)** following the death of his brother **Rajyavardhan** and the murder of his brother-in-law **Grahavarman**. His accession is traditionally reckoned as the start of the **Harsha era**.

**Unification of the north:** His first campaign was against **Shashanka of Gauda**, to avenge Rajyavardhan and recover his sister **Rajyashri**; allying with **Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa**, he defeated Shashanka. He then claimed **Kannauj**, **united Thanesar and Kannauj**, and made **Kannauj his capital**. He brought **Punjab and central India** under control, **annexed Bengal, Bihar and Odisha**, and defeated the **Vallabhi king in Gujarat** — welding a patchwork of feudatories into a single paramount power.

**Failure in the south:** Harsha's northern success met its limit at the **Deccan**. The **Chalukya king Pulakeshin II** defeated him in **618–619 CE**, restricting his territory to the **Narmada River**. The rising tide of **feudalism** — powerful land-granted nobles and feudatory kings — also limited effective central control.

**Assessment:** Harsha reunified the Gangetic heartland after the fall of the Guptas and gave northern India a generation of **peace and prosperity**, but his empire rested on personal authority over feudatories rather than a durable administrative structure — a weakness exposed both by Pulakeshin II and by the empire's collapse after his heirless death.
keyPoints: Pushyabhuti/Vardhana dynasty; born 590 CE at Thanesar; accession c. 606 CE (Harsha era).
First campaign vs Shashanka of Gauda; alliance with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa.
United Thanesar & Kannauj (capital Kannauj); annexed Bengal, Bihar, Odisha; defeated Vallabhi (Gujarat).
Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha (618–619 CE); southern limit fixed at the Narmada.
Growing feudalism weakened central control; empire rested on personal paramountcy.

items.question: Discuss Harshavardhana's contribution to literature, learning and religion, with reference to Banabhatta, Hiuen-Tsang, Nalanda and the great assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag.
items.modelAnswer:
Harsha's reign was as notable for its **cultural efflorescence** as for its conquests, making him a landmark patron of the arts and religion.

**Harsha as author:** A scholar himself, Harsha wrote **three Sanskrit plays** — **Ratnavali** (a four-act drama of princess Ratnavali and King Udayana, with an early reference to Holi), **Priyadarshika** and **Nagananda** (Buddhist in theme).

**Literary patronage — Banabhatta:** His court poet **Banabhatta** wrote the **Harshacharita** ('Deeds of Harsha'), a verse biography that is a prime source for the reign, and **Kadambari**, among the world's earliest novels.

**Hiuen-Tsang and Nalanda:** The Chinese pilgrim **Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang)** spent about **13 years in India (630–643 CE)**; his **Si-Yu-Ki** vividly records the social, economic and religious life of the age, praising **Nalanda** as the leading university — an institution Harsha generously patronised. He noted **Prayag and Kanauj** rising as centres while Pataliputra and Vaishali declined.

**Religion and assemblies:** Originally a Shaiva, Harsha came under the influence of his sister **Rajyashri** and of Buddhist monks and embraced **Mahayana Buddhism**, yet remained a **secular ruler** respecting all faiths. He convened a great **assembly at Kannauj** honouring Hiuen-Tsang and promoting Mahayana, and the famous **charitable convocation at Prayag**, where he distributed the royal treasury as alms.

**Conclusion:** Through his own writings, the patronage of Banabhatta, the support of Nalanda and the grand assemblies, Harsha presided over one of the high points of early medieval Indian culture, remembered long after his empire dissolved.
keyPoints: Harsha authored three plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda (Ratnavali in four acts, refers to Holi).
Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita (verse biography) and Kadambari (early novel).
Hiuen-Tsang (630–643 CE) wrote the Si-Yu-Ki; praised Nalanda, the leading university Harsha patronised.
Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen-Tsang & promoted Mahayana; Prayag assembly was a great charitable convocation.
Shaiva turned Mahayana Buddhist yet secular — respected all faiths.

items.question: Examine the administrative and revenue system of Harshavardhana and explain how the growth of feudalism shaped the character and decline of his empire.
items.modelAnswer:
Harsha's administration combined a **strong central monarchy** with an increasingly **feudalised and decentralised** structure — a tension that ultimately shaped the empire's fate.

**Administrative structure:** As supreme ruler, Harsha centralised key military and administrative decisions, assisted by a **Mantri Parishad (Council of Ministers)** that even had a voice in policy. The empire was divided into provinces (**Bhuktis**) under **Governors**, districts (**Vishayas**) under **Vishayapatis**, and villages under headmen (**Gramikas**). Key officials included **Avanti** (foreign relations and war), **Simhanada** (Commander-in-Chief), **Kuntala** (cavalry), **Skandagupta** (elephant force) and **Sarvagata** (secret service). A large army — reportedly **100,000 cavalry, 50,000 infantry and 60,000 elephants** — upheld his authority.

**Revenue system:** Three principal taxes were levied — **Bhaga** (land tax, one-sixth of produce), **Hiranya** (cash tax from farmers and merchants) and **Bali** (an additional, oppressive levy). Revenue was divided into four parts — for the state, for officers, for men of letters, and for charity — with about **25% spent on charity and cultural purposes**.

**Feudalism and decline:** The practice of **rewarding officers and religious figures (Brahmins, Buddhists) with land grants (Agraharas)** decentralised revenue and judicial power; this is why **few coins** survive from Harsha's reign. Land-holding became a mark of social superiority, and feudal lords grew powerful enough to **defy orders and withhold taxes**. After Harsha's **heirless death in 647 CE**, these very feudatories broke away, and the empire **disintegrated into smaller regional kingdoms**.

**Conclusion:** Harsha's polity worked while his personal authority held it together, but the feudalising forces it relied upon carried the seeds of its fragmentation — a foreshadowing of the political order of early medieval India.
keyPoints: Strong central king + Mantri Parishad; Bhuktis (Governors), Vishayas (Vishayapatis), villages (Gramikas).
Officials: Avanti (war/foreign), Simhanada (C-in-C), Kuntala (cavalry), Skandagupta (elephants), Sarvagata (secret service).
Taxes: Bhaga (land, 1/6), Hiranya (cash), Bali (additional); ~25% of revenue for charity/culture.
Land grants (Agraharas) decentralised power; few coins issued.
Heirless death in 647 CE + feudatory revolts caused disintegration into regional kingdoms.
